name: Cellulite lasers / Cellfina

card.summary: Office procedures that cut or heat the bands behind cellulite dimples; one subcision device has 3-year follow-up data, but evidence for lasers is thinner.
card.note: Best suited to dimple-type cellulite according to treating clinicians.

quick.overview:
Cellfina is a device-guided subcision procedure for dimple-type cellulite. Laser and other energy devices are discussed alongside it as options.
A pivotal study followed Cellfina patients for three years and reported sustained improvement.
quick.mechanism: Subcision releases the fibrous bands that tether the skin and create dimples; Cellfina does this with a tissue-stabilized, guided device.
quick.risks: It is a minimally invasive in-office procedure; clinicians note patient selection matters because not all body contour concerns are dimple-type cellulite.

lead: Cellulite lasers and Cellfina are in-office procedures aimed at the dimpled skin surface that many people, mostly women, notice on the thighs and buttocks. Cellfina is a tissue-stabilized, guided subcision (TS-GS) device that mechanically releases the fibrous bands under the skin that are associated with dimple-type cellulite, with the aim of smoothing the surface.[1][3] Laser and other energy-based devices are a separate group of treatments discussed alongside it.[5][6]

People seek these treatments to reduce the visible dimpling on the legs and buttocks so skin looks smoother in swimwear or fitted clothes. A pivotal open-label multicenter study followed 45 Cellfina patients for up to three years after a single treatment and reported sustained improvement in the appearance of cellulite.[1] Treating clinicians note that the device is best suited to dimple-type cellulite and that patients often label other body features as cellulite.[3]

A 2015 dermatology review describes cellulite as of no danger to overall health but potentially psychosocially burdensome, and examined topical treatments, noninvasive energy-based devices and newer minimally invasive interventions.[7] Published research on lasers specifically for cellulite is thinner than the Cellfina follow-up data.

chain: Needle-sized device releases the fibrous bands that pull the skin down
Dimples are less visible as the skin surface relaxes
angle.text: A clinician uses subcision to cut the fibrous septae that tether the skin and create dimples, or applies laser or other energy to heat tissue. People use these procedures to reduce the look of dimple-type cellulite.

paras: Cellulite is a common cosmetic concern in women, and a 2017 pivotal-study paper described no single treatment as having been proven effective over the long term before the tissue stabilized-guided subcision (TS-GS) system appeared.[1] Wikipedia lists laser and pulsed-light treatments, subcision, radiofrequency, ultrasound, cryotherapy and collagenase injections among options used, and notes that cellulite can be resistant to many treatments.[5]

Subcision cuts the fibrous bands that pull on the skin surface. It can be done manually with a needle-sized microscalpel, with vacuum assistance, or with laser assistance, in specialist clinics under local anaesthetic.[5] Cellfina is described in a Canadian retrospective evaluation as the first FDA-cleared, long-lasting, minimally invasive device for improving cellulite appearance.[4]
Subcision is also a general technique used for deep rolling scars such as those left by acne, in which the skin is detached from tethering scar tissue underneath.[8]

Cellfina combines a vacuum-assisted skin-stabilising handpiece with a small blade that is guided under the skin to release the fibrous septae that tether the surface and produce a dimple. Because the cut is made at a fixed depth under local anaesthetic through a needle-sized entry, the procedure is described as minimally invasive and is done in a single office visit.[3][4]

The structural idea behind it is that dimple-type cellulite is caused by connective-tissue bands that pull skin down while fat herniates between them. Releasing a band allows the overlying skin to rise, which is the chain from the procedure to a smoother surface. This is different from approaches that try to change fat volume, and different again from topical products and massage.[3][5]

Energy-based treatments include radiofrequency, ultrasound, cryotherapy and laser or pulsed-light systems, and clinics often combine mechanical and energy-based methods.[5] DermNet describes laser-assisted lipolysis using Nd:YAG lasers as possibly suitable for small areas of fat but perhaps less effective for cellulite than liposuction is for large deposits, and says radiofrequency devices have shown mixed but sometimes impressive results in small studies, with long-term efficacy unknown.[9] The same page says liposuction is not recommended for cellulite because the fat is near the surface and cosmetic results are poor.[9]

Wikipedia's overview of cellulite notes that it can resist many treatments and lists creams and ointments, collagenase injections, suction and massage, radiofrequency, ultrasound, cryotherapy and laser or pulsed-light systems among the approaches used, often in combination.[5] Laser-assisted subcision uses a laser fibre introduced under the skin to release bands and heat the tissue, and is one of the ways energy is paired with subcision.[5]

Clinicians who have shared their experience with Cellfina say it most effectively treats dimple-type cellulite, where fibrous bands inserting into the underside of the skin create a puckered look, and that prospective patients should be educated about this because many consider any undesirable feature from the knees to the umbilicus, and even the arms, to be cellulite.[3]

Wikipedia reports that cellulite is estimated to affect 80 to 90% of post-adolescent women in European populations, is considerably less common in East Asian women, and is rarely seen in men. Many factors are implicated, including connective tissue structure, hormones, genetics, body fat and lifestyle, and medical opinion generally treats it as a normal physiological condition.[5] DermNet describes it as fat pushing into the dermis and lists genetics, hormones, sex, ethnicity, diet, body weight and prolonged sitting or standing as possible contributors.[9]
The term originated in spa and beauty services in the 1920s and entered English-language publications in the late 1960s; a 1978 paper called it an invented disease.[5]

Wikipedia describes cellulite as herniation of subcutaneous fat within fibrous connective tissue and as a physiological rather than pathological feature. It lists metabolism, diet and exercise habits, hormones, connective-tissue structure and genetics among the contributors, and says that although oestrogen is often proposed as a factor, there is no reliable clinical evidence linking oestrogen levels to cellulite.[5]

DermNet notes that needle subcision may only temporarily reduce dimpling and that long-term results are uncertain, and lists adverse effects for some other approaches such as mesotherapy (abscesses, scarring, worsened dimpling).[9] The Cellfina studies report on efficacy and satisfaction as described in the clinical studies section.
Soreness, tenderness and bruising were the most commonly reported effects after Cellfina in the pivotal data summarised in the clearance announcement.[10]

A multicenter pivotal study of the TS-GS system reported significant reductions in the appearance of cellulite. In the extended follow-up, 45 subjects who had received a single treatment were followed for up to three years in an open-label design in which subjects served as their own controls, with photographs assessed by blinded independent reviewers.[1]

A multicenter retrospective evaluation from two early Canadian sites analysed the charts of female patients treated in 2017, with baseline and 3-month measurements of patient satisfaction and physician-rated efficacy, in the first year the device was on the market in Canada.[4] A registered trial of a different device, the Cabochon system, enrolled 55 participants beginning in 2012 for cellulite appearance.[2]

The Cellfina system, made by Merz Aesthetics, received FDA clearance for long-term improvement of cellulite on the buttocks and thighs of adult women, with a three-year indication reported in October 2016 on the basis of a prospective multicentre US study of 55 patients treated once.[10] The manufacturer reported improvement in 98 percent of patients at three years as rated by independent physician evaluators and satisfaction in 93 percent of patients; these figures come from the company's announcement of the clearance, and no serious device-related adverse events were reported in the pivotal trial and follow-up.[10]

timeline.event: The term cellulite is first used by spa and beauty services.[5]
Registered trial of the Cabochon system begins (55 participants).[2]
Three-year follow-up of the Cellfina pivotal study (45 subjects) is published.[1]
Retrospective evaluation of first-year Canadian experience with TS-GS is published.[4]
